summary: Technical deep-dive focusing on GPU runtime performance profiling for Aurora's 8B/70B LLMs. Topics: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA Graphs for steady-state, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization compatibility, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed to run reproducible pilot and share traces and configs.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Sam: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna do a deep dive on GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, tensorrt-llm vs vllm, and how cuda graphs and kv caching affect latency and throughput. we have erin on the call to go into the traces.
[00:00:18] Maya: thanks Sam, excited — we mainly want to understand how we'd get stable p95 latency under 200ms for chat workloads and how caching affects cost. we run a mix of 8B for low-latency and 70B for high-quality generation.
[00:00:32] Erin: yep that's the right framing, and we dug into the initial traces you sent. there are a few hotspots which look like kernel selection mismatches and some fragmentation in cu graph warm-up, we'll show some nvprof screenshots.
[00:00:48] Diego: quick note — our traffic profile is very spiky, 90% short sequences <64 tokens but 5-10% long sessions up to 1024 tokens; burstiness is the issue.
[00:00:58] Priya: also, we have a strict VPC + KMS setup; on-prem might be required for a subset of PII workloads.
[00:01:07] Sam: got it, we'll cover VPC/private and how dedicated pools behave with KV cache and autoscale. erin, can you start with the high-level perf slide?
[00:01:14] Erin: sure. slide share... ok first thing: kernel selection — our runtime probes model op shapes at load and during warm-up. if the kernel library picks a generic matmul kernel instead of the fused attention one, you'll see 2-3x slowdowns on attention layers especially for 70B. we saw this in your 70B runs — some attention kernels fell back to slower paths because of sequence length changes.
[00:01:45] Maya: is that vllm behavior or our infra? we thought vllm did some kernel autotune.
[00:01:52] Erin: vLLM has good defaults but it doesn't always pick vendor-specific fused kernels like TensorRT-LLM can. TensorRT-LLM includes optimized fused attention and gelu kernels and usually gives better throughput on stable sequence lengths, but it's more sensitive to dynamic sequence length changes and kv cache patterns.
[00:02:11] Diego: so tradeoff is throughput vs latency stability?
[00:02:15] Erin: exactly. vLLM is more flexible and tends to be robust at low batch and variable seq lengths; TensorRT-LLM gives higher throughput at the cost of warm-up time and sometimes higher p95 for tailcases when graphs recompile.
[00:02:27] Sam: i want to call out cuda graphs — we saw a lot of people confuse cu-graphs with a silver bullet. they help reduce CPU overhead and scheduling jitter for steady-state loops, but they require consistent execution graphs. with variable-length requests or frequent kv cache flushes, graphs need to be re-captured which adds jitter.
[00:02:45] Priya: so for our spiky profile, would you recommend cuda graphs?
[00:02:48] Erin: yes, but in a hybrid way. use cuda graphs for the common short-seq path — capture a few representative lengths (16, 32, 64) and dispatch to pre-captured graphs for those. for long tails or dynamic requests, fall back to the flexible runtime path (vLLM-like). that gives you the low p99 for the common case and controlled tail for the rest.
[00:03:07] Maya: how many graphs do you typically capture? storage or memory overhead?
[00:03:12] Erin: 3-6 graphs is typical; memory overhead is negligible relative to model KV cache, it's mostly a small GPU memory reservation for the captured kernel sequences. more important is managing compilation time and ensuring graphs map to the right kernel selection.
[00:03:27] Diego: we saw spikes where attention kernels recompiled mid-run, causing a 400ms tail. any quick wins to avoid that?
[00:03:33] Erin: yes — pin the model micro-batch and sequence length during the capture window, and preload the fused kernel libraries before traffic. for TensorRT-LLM, pre-warm with representative inputs so it doesn't fall back. also lock the cuDNN and TensorRT versions to tested combos — we keep a matrix.
[00:03:51] Sam: i'll share our kernel-version compatibility matrix; erin has a sample.
[00:03:55] Erin: right, i'll upload the matrix to the shared drive: link (https://redwood-internal.example.com/aurora/perf-matrix).
[00:04:03] Maya: on KV cache — we want to leverage prefix caching to reduce tokens generated and latency for multi-turn chat. but concerned about cache invalidation semantics for multi-tenant models.
[00:04:15] Erin: our KV cache supports per-tenant namespaces and TTL-based eviction. the common pattern is to cache transformer KV per conversation id and reuse for short-turn messages. the tricky bit is memory fragmentation when conversation counts grow — you can either use sharded caches per GPU or a tiered approach: in-GPU hot cache + remote Redis-style cold cache.
[00:04:34] Priya: remote cache adds network hop; what's the latency impact?
[00:04:38] Erin: remote cache adds ~0.5-3ms depending on network; compared to a 20-30ms attention compute it's often acceptable for cold misses. but for strict p95 targets under 200ms, aim to keep hot cache in-GPU for top 90% traffic.
[00:04:51] Diego: quantization — we saw some quality regressions when moving to int8 on our 8B model. are there recommended profiles?
[00:04:58] Erin: quantization profiles matter: per-channel asymmetric quant works better for attention weights; calibration with your workload is essential. TensorRT-LLM supports QAT-ish workflows and calibrated int8 with minimal quality loss if you provide a representative dataset. vLLM's fbgemm/quant paths are good too but may lack some fused kernels.
[00:05:16] Maya: can you run a quick demo of a trace you saw?
[00:05:20] Erin: sure — pulling up nvprof trace.
[00:05:23] Erin: [screen] here is your 70B baseline: note the attention kernel blocks around 00:10–00:12 in the trace (we'll annotate). the kernel chosen was a fallback matmul path; if you switch to TensorRT-LLM with fused attention we saw runtime drop ~45% in throughput for fixed batch but p95 variation increased on long tails.
[00:05:46] Maya: did you repro with our exact model and tokenization?
[00:05:50] Erin: yes we used your model artifact and same tokenizer; small mismatches happen if tokenization differs, so please share any local patches.
[00:05:58] Diego: you mentioned fragmentation from KV cache — any tooling to surface per-GPU KV memory usage?
[00:06:03] Erin: our console shows per-GPU KV usage with histograms and evictions; we'll share screenshots. quick tip: enable periodic compaction on idle windows and enforce per-conversation max-kv to avoid one chat hogging memory.
[00:06:18] Sam: quick interruption — Maya, what's your target p95 today; you said <200ms but is that for 8B only or both models?
[00:06:26] Maya: primarily 8B interactive; for 70B we can accept higher p95 if throughput is good — we want p95 < 500ms for 70B.
[00:06:33] Sam: ok that helps; so our hybrid graph approach + in-GPU hot caching for 8B should hit that.
[00:06:39] Priya: network: our VPC uses strict egress rules (no outbound to internet); any agents need that?
[00:06:45] Sam: for Private you can run the control plane in a Red-allowed subnet; Dedicated can be setup VPC-peered or via Transit Gateway; we support customer-managed KMS and on-prem installers if needed.
[00:06:57] Erin: operational notes: on-prem brings additional constraints — driver/kernel versions, GPU firmware and MIG configs matter. we recommend a preflight checklist and we can run a validation agent to capture system telemetry.
[00:07:10] Diego: about MIG — we run A100s with 40G and sometimes partition. does MIG affect CUDA Graphs behavior?
[00:07:16] Erin: MIG introduces isolation but also changes scheduling; CUDA Graphs still works but you need to capture graphs per-MIG slice because SM count and scheduler differs. often we avoid heavy graph reliance on MIG partitions unless it's stable.
[00:07:29] Maya: curious about autoscaling interactions — you said graphs require stable execution, but autoscale will spin up new nodes. how do we keep warm nodes?
[00:07:36] Erin: we have two approaches: keep a small warm pool (reserved GPUs) for steady-state and use fast warm-up for bursts, or do predictive pre-warming based on traffic forecasting. Dedicated includes options for reserved capacity and burst buffers.
[00:07:51] Sam: i'll include pricing for reserved capacity vs pure on-demand.
[00:07:55] Diego: can you quantify warm-up time for a 70B model to get optimized kernels and graphs loaded?
[00:08:01] Erin: depends on model and infra. for 70B with TensorRT-LLM warm-up can be 2-6 minutes to compile and capture graphs; vLLM flexible path is usually <30s but won’t hit the same steady-state throughput. that's why for latency-sensitive short sessions we prefer 8B on the fused graph path and route long queries to the flexible 70B pool.
[00:08:18] Maya: routing — can Redwood automatically route by latency profile?
[00:08:22] Sam: yes, our smart routing can tag requests by intent, seq length, and SLA and route to different model variants or pools; you can set fallback policies. we'll show config snippets.
[00:08:31] Erin: here's an example: route short reqs (<64 tokens) to 8B graph-captured pool; route >64 tokens to vLLM flexible or to a TensorRT-LLM 70B dedicated pool depending on quality need.
[00:08:44] Priya: security question: logs — can we redact tokens or disable transcript logging for PII?
[00:08:50] Sam: yes, in Private mode you control retention, and we offer token redaction and fine-grained audit logging; we can disable storing raw prompts and only store metrics.
[00:08:59] Diego: any gotchas on quantization with TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM?
[00:09:03] Erin: TensorRT has advanced int8 support but you must provide a representative calibration dataset; if your distribution is skewed (lots of code vs natural text) calibrate accordingly. vLLM quant options are easier to iterate but may not reach the same speed for large models.
[00:09:16] Maya: what about mixed precision (fp16) vs int8?
[00:09:19] Erin: fp16 is the safe first step: good speedups with minimal quality loss. int8 gives more compression but requires careful calibration. for production we often go fp16 first, then selective int8 for less-sensitive layers.
[00:09:32] Sam: let's talk about a reproducible benchmark — we'll need: model artifact, tokenizer, representative payloads, seq length distribution, target SLA, and candidate infra. erin will provide the benchmark harness.
[00:09:43] Erin: yes, we'll share a harness script that runs both vLLM and TensorRT-LLM flows and captures kernel-level traces, cuda graph capture/fallbacks, and kv cache hit rates. it will output p50/p95/p99 and per-kernel timings.
[00:09:56] Diego: can that run in our environment (on-prem)?
[00:09:58] Erin: yes the harness can run in Private mode or as a self-contained docker with privileged nv* access. we'll provide instructions.
[00:10:05] Maya: any reference numbers we can expect for 8B fp16 on A100?
[00:10:09] Erin: ballpark: with fused kernels and graphs you can get per-GPU throughput of ~60-150 tokens/sec depending on batch; p95 for short seqs can be under 50ms if hot cache present. without fused kernels expect 2-3x higher latency. these are rough and depend heavily on sequence length and batch.
[00:10:27] Priya: ok good.
[00:10:29] Sam: i want to surface one more operational note: kernel mismatches sometimes come from mismatched CUDA/TensorRT versions across nodes — we recommend an immutable image for Dedicated and Private to avoid drift.
[00:10:40] Erin: also watch out for pinned NUMA configs and CPU affinity; GPU performance can be affected by host-level scheduling.
[00:10:47] Diego: good to know.
[00:10:50] Maya: last question on model variants — can we serve quantized 8B for general users and route certain customers to full 70B?
[00:10:56] Sam: yes that's a common pattern — model aliasing and routing by customer or route. Redwood Console shows per-route cost and latency so you can audit.
[00:11:05] Erin: okay i'm going to share the trace folder link now — (https://redwood-internal.example.com/aurora/perf-traces) — contains NVPROF, cudagraphs captures, and sample harness runs.
[00:11:16] Diego: thanks, we'll pull those.
[00:11:20] Sam: let's recap next steps: erin uploads traces + matrix (you did), sam sends pricing and SOW, diego shares config and sample payloads, schedule pilot.
[00:11:29] Maya: yep sounds good.
[00:11:32] Priya: we'll confirm network constraints and KMS.
[00:11:35] Sam: great, we'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot start and a checklist.
[00:11:40] Erin: any other questions?
[00:11:43] Maya: not right now, thanks everyone.
[00:11:46] Diego: thanks.
[00:11:48] Sam: thanks, bye.
[00:11:52] (end of recorded segment)
